item.mechanism: Grain refinement during dual-beam irradiation is caused by high-energy recoil events creating sub-cascades that fragment grains into sub-grains, an effect enabled because the cascade size is comparable to the initial nanocrystalline grain size.
item.system: Quinary W29.4Ta42Cr5.0V16.1Hf7.5 nanocrystalline RHEA thin film
item.operating_conditions: Dual-beam irradiation with 1-MeV Kr+ and 16 keV He+ at 1173 K; single-beam He implantation at 1173 K showed grain growth instead
item.supporting_observation: Grain size dropped from 24.5 nm to 21.1 nm during dual-beam irradiation, while He-only implantation increased grain size to 36.3 nm; in situ TEM video captured grain fragmentation.
item.scope_limits: Mechanism does not apply to single-beam He implantation (causes growth) or coarser-grained materials where cascades are smaller than grains; specific to nanocrystalline grains near 10-25 nm.
item.alternatives_considered: Defect clusters migrating to sub-grain boundaries forming cell structures; cascades larger than grain size forming stacking faults (observed in FCC materials).
quotes: Molecular dynamics simulations have shown that high-energy (50 keV) recoil events begin to divide in sub-cascades [34] , [35] , each with a diameter on the order of 10 nm.

This upper limit on cascade size is near the initial grain-size of the W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA, allowing fragmentation to take place whereas, in coarser-grained materials, a similar event would likely result in defect migration to boundaries.
Grain refinement was not observed for the He only case, but rather grain growth occurred as shown in Fig. 3 .

item.mechanism: Homogenization of chemical distribution and suppression of precipitation occur because irradiation-induced ballistic mixing and atomic displacement drive the system past the Order-Disorder Transition Temperature (ODTT), eliminating short-range order.
item.system: Quinary W31Ta34Cr5.0V27Hf3.0 thick film and W29.4Ta42Cr5.0V16.1Hf7.5 thin film
item.operating_conditions: Irradiation at 1073 K (ex situ) and 1173 K (in situ); ODTT values of ~1120 K and ~1080 K respectively
item.supporting_observation: APT showed homogenization in irradiated samples with no precipitation, unlike the quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V alloy which showed Cr-V precipitation; SRO parameters approached zero at irradiation temperatures.
item.scope_limits: Does not hold at temperatures significantly below the ODTT where ordering and precipitation (e.g., Cr-Hf) are predicted; composition changes can alter ODTT and SRO behavior.
item.alternatives_considered: Formation of Cr-V precipitates as seen in the quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA; segregation of Hf to grain boundaries during annealing.
quotes: Homogenization of the elements occurs when all SRO values tend to zero which marks the ODTT of the alloy.
The W 31 Ta 34 Cr 5 V 27 Hf 3.0 showed an ODTT of ~1120 K which roughly coincides with the irradiation temperature.
Considering the irradiation-induced ballistic mixing and the corresponding atomic displacement and ordering [37] , homogenization can occur at lower temperatures.

item.mechanism: High irradiation resistance (no dislocation loops, small bubbles) is attributed to a rough energy landscape where He has a higher tendency to find stable sites and bind to other He atoms, slowing clustering and promoting uniform distribution.
item.operating_conditions: Dual-beam irradiation (1 MeV Kr+ + 16 keV He+) and single-beam He implantation at 1173 K up to 8.5 dpa and ~9% He
item.supporting_observation: No dislocation loops detected after 8.5 dpa; cavities saturated early; He migration energy (0.156 eV) is higher than in pure W, leading to slower He mobility and smaller bubbles.
item.scope_limits: Mechanism relies on specific He migration energies and formation energies calculated for this system; may not apply if defect migration barriers change significantly with composition.
item.alternatives_considered: High interstitial-vacancy recombination; lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion effects; difficulty of defect clustering.
quotes: This rough energy landscape implies that He has a higher tendency to quickly find a fairly stable site that can act as a bubble nuclei, and also to bind to other slowly migrating He interstitial atoms.
The He average migration energy was found to be 0.156 eV in the alloy compared to 0.06 to 0.081 eV in pure W and the He formation energy was approximately 2 times lower [47] , [48] .

The clustering of He will slow them further down and a trend for smaller and lesser bubble nucleation will follow, and therefore, uniform bubble distribution with no preferential bubble formation at the grain boundaries or a wide distribution of bubble sizes occur.

item.mechanism: Increased hardness after annealing is caused by Hf segregation to grain boundaries, which acts as a strengthening mechanism distinct from irradiation effects.
item.operating_conditions: Annealing at 1173 K for ~30 mins in TEM; hardness measured via nanoindentation
item.supporting_observation: Hardness increased from 13.25 GPa to 16.25 GPa after annealing; EDX showed Hf segregation to grain boundaries after annealing.
item.scope_limits: Specific to the annealing process; does not explain the additional hardness increase observed after irradiation.
item.alternatives_considered: Lattice distortion or grain refinement (which are irradiation effects, not annealing effects).
quotes: Increase in hardness after annealing is solely associated with Hf segregation along the GBs whereas the increase after irradiation is a synergistic combination between Ar implantation, lattice distortion caused by irradiation ballistic mixing, and grain refinement.
The increase in hardness after annealing was ~3 GPa and this can be directly attributed to Hf segregation to grain boundaries as revealed in Fig. 2 and in the STEM-EDX mapping as insets in Fig. 5 .

item.mechanism: Hardness increase after irradiation is a synergistic result of Ar implantation, lattice distortion from homogenization, and grain refinement, rather than a single mechanism.
item.operating_conditions: Ex situ irradiation with 400 keV Ar+2 ions at 1073 K to 10 dpa; nanoindentation at 200 nm depth
item.supporting_observation: Hardness reached 20 GPa after irradiation; the increase correlates with the peak of Ar implantation and the transition from ordered to disordered state.
item.scope_limits: Specific to the depth profile where Ar implantation peaks (~200 nm); beyond this depth, the difference between irradiated and annealed curves decreases.
item.alternatives_considered: Dispersed barrier hardening (DBH) from invisible defect clusters; solely due to elemental segregation.
quotes: This RHEA possesses high irradiation resistance and shows no dislocation loop formation, even under dual-beam conditions (where He can bind to vacancies allowing interstitials to coalesce faster).
This change is higher when the grain size is very small and approaches the edge of the transition from the Hall-Petch to the Inverse Hall-Petch effect [55] .

At the peak of the Ar irradiation/implantation profile (~200 nm), the hardness increase is a result of a synergistic combination of Ar implantation, lattice distortion, and grain refinement, thus not solely due to one specific cause.

item.mechanism: Grain boundaries act as defect sinks, but the dominant factor for irradiation resistance in this nanocrystalline HEA is the grain matrix chemistry rather than the grain boundary area itself.
item.system: Nanocrystalline W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA compared to coarse grain HEA and pure W
item.operating_conditions: Irradiation environments with high atomic percentage of He implantation at 1173 K
item.supporting_observation: No preferential bubble formation at grain boundaries despite high He content; surface ratio is approximately 10, yet surface effects are smaller than in pure W.
item.scope_limits: Does not negate the role of grain boundaries as sinks; specifically notes that the matrix chemistry is the dominant factor compared to the grain boundary contribution.
item.alternatives_considered: Grain boundaries being the primary sink for defects; surface effects dominating due to high surface-to-volume ratio.
quotes: Grain boundaries can also play a role in the irradiation resistance of the alloy acting as defect sinks.

The contribution of grain boundaries, however, compared to grain matrices to the irradiation resistance has been studied comparing NC HEA and coarse grain HEA to NC-W and coarse grain W and it was found that the dominant factor is the grain matrix chemistry [49] .
Furthermore, surface effects in the RHEA system are expected to be smaller than in pure W due to the rougher defect migration landscapes in HEAs [42] .

item.mechanism: The addition of Hf lowers the valence electron concentration (VEC) to below 4.4, promoting the formation of a single-phase BCC structure and enhancing mechanical stability.
item.operating_conditions: Thermodynamic design stage using CALPHAD and VEC model; predicted to form single-phase BCC over a wide temperature range
item.supporting_observation: CALPHAD predicted single-phase BCC structure; VEC value of 5.2 was the minimum achievable with Hf addition, favoring single-phase formation.
item.scope_limits: The VEC value of 4.4 is based on a few works and is not considered an absolute number; specific to the W-Ta-Cr-V base system modified with Group IV elements.
item.alternatives_considered: Replacing V with Fe (failed due to intermetallic phase formation and lower melting point); other Group IV elements (Ti, Zr) not selected due to Hf's high melting point.
quotes: It has been shown that BCC RHEAs can exhibit high-stability and suitable mechanical properties when the VEC value remains below 4.4 [24] , [25] .
Group IV elements can then be used to pursue this approach (e.g., Ti, Zr, and Hf) and modify the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA.

Due to its high melting point, Hf was firstly selected with a minimal concentration to avoid a material with high activation under in-reactor conditions and to maximize the probability of obtaining a single-phase HEA.

item.mechanism: Depletion of Hf from grain boundaries during irradiation is caused by the Inverse Kirkendall effect (IKE) and/or ballistic mixing.
item.operating_conditions: Dual-beam irradiation and He implantation at 1173 K; annealing at 1173 K prior to irradiation
item.supporting_observation: EDX analysis showed Hf concentration decreases at grain boundaries after irradiation compared to the annealed sample where Hf had segregated there.
item.scope_limits: Specific to Hf depletion; other elements (V, Cr) showed inhomogeneous distribution but the specific mechanism for Hf is IKE/ballistic mixing.
item.alternatives_considered: Segregation of Hf to grain boundaries during annealing (the opposite effect observed before irradiation).
quotes: The EDX demonstrated depletion of Hf from grain boundaries during irradiation which can be attributed to the Inverse Kirkendall effect (IKE) [36] and/or ballistic mixing during irradiation [37] .
After annealing, Hf segregates to grain boundaries, and V and Cr are also inhomogeneously distributed throughout the sample, thus indicating segregation.
After irradiation, Hf starts to deplete from the grain boundaries (Hf concentration decreases compared to the annealed sample).
